**Limb Architecture & Degrees of Freedom Research**

**Objective**  
Develop a two-segment limb structure modelled after the human arm. Define the precise lengths for each subsection and map out the required degrees of freedom (DoF) to ensure the arm can reach its intended workspace using servo motor joints.

**Segment Length and Ratios**  
Empirical measurements of the human arm provide a strong reference for designing and functional robotic systems. According to data found on [this research](https://multisite.eos.ncsu.edu/www-ergocenter-ncsu-edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/18/2016/06/Anthropometric-Detailed-Data-Tables.pdf), the mean elbow-wrist length ranges from 26.25cm to 29.30cm while the mean shoulder-elbow length ranges from 33.58 to 36.90cm. From these values, we can estimate that the ratio between the length of the upper arm and the length of the forearm is approximately 1: 0.8-0.9.                                              

Mimicking this proportion in a robotic system can help avoid unnecessary limitations in workspace. For example, if our upper arm is 30cm while our forearm is only 15 cm, then the minimum reachable radius becomes around 15cm. (Minimum reach ≈ upper arm length − forearm length). This creates a dead zone near the base where the arm cannot reach. 

Additional consequences of poor ratios include reduced influence of the elbow joint on end position, lower precision and dexterity, and less controllable motion overall. While a shorter forearm can help reduce torque requirements at the elbow joint, this advantage is easily outweighed by the loss in functionality. Selecting motors capable of delivering greater torque instead would be a way better option.

**Degree of Freedom (DoF) Considerations**  
An ideal robotic arm would possess full spatial manipulation capabilities with 6 degrees of freedom (DoF), consisting of three translational axes (x, y, z) and three rotational axes (roll, pitch, yaw). However, due to budget constraints, it is preferred that the design utilizes as few motors as possible while still remaining fully functional for its intended application. 

As a result, our limb design will prioritize rotational degrees of freedom. This is justified based on the following reasons:

1. Rotational degrees of freedom are needed for high precision and dexterity.  
2. Given that the robot arm only needs to reach a point no farther than a 30cm radius, we can simply increase the lengths of the upper arm and the forearm, so that we do not need the entire robot to translate horizontally or vertically to reach a point.

Simply put, the location of the base of the robot arm will be fixed. However, the robot can move its upper arm and forearm freely (rotational motion through the application of motors on joints). This results in a simplified but still functional arm capable of reaching a wide workspace.

**Additional Concerns / Information**  
The primary design goal is for the arm to reach any point within a 30cm radius from its base. To ensure reliability and avoid operating at maximum extension, we should incorporate a 20-30% safety margin, so the target maximum reach would be around 36-39cm. Although the maximum reach required has not been finalized yet as of 21/03/2026, the segments can be easily scaled proportionally without disrupting the system’s performance if a greater/shorter reach is preferred.
